title: What Kind of Recruiter Do You Need? (September 2026)
summary: Compare agency, fractional, in-house, and RPO recruiters to see which model fits your startup's hiring goals. Updated September 2026.
body_markdown:
Agency recruiters are fast but expensive and misaligned by design. A[full-time in-house hire](https://www.dover.com/) is embedded but needs enough volume to warrant the cost. A solo fractional recruiter is flexible but one sick day away from stalling your pipeline. If you’re trying to figure out which of these actually fits your company right now, the decision comes down to a few specific variables worth thinking through carefully.


**TLDR:**


-


Agency recruiters charge 15-25% of first-year salary on contingency, which can misalign incentives toward speed over fit.


-


In-house recruiters carry $85,000-$170,000/year in loaded costs and only make economic sense at 15-20 hires per year.


-


Fractional recruiters cost less but are a single point of failure with limited tooling and no backup support.


-


Some tools pair free ATS software with on-demand recruiting support averaging about $4,800 per hire instead of fixed retainers.


-


The right model depends on your hiring volume, growth stage, and how much fixed cost your runway can absorb.


## Where Most Hiring Headaches Actually Start


Typically, the first thing you need help with is sourcing: finding more high quality candidates you actually want to interview.


With AI tools now handling scheduling, screening, and note-taking across most of these models, the recruiter model you choose shapes how well those tools get applied to your specific hiring bar. As of September 2026, startups are increasingly mixing fractional support with in-house AI tooling to keep costs down without sacrificing quality.


Model Cost Structure Best For Key Tradeoff


Agency Recruiter 15-25% of first-year salary (contingency) One-off or urgent single hires Incentives favor speed over fit; high cost per hire


In-House Recruiter $85,000-$170,000/year loaded cost (per[SHRM benchmarking](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/recruiting-benchmarking) ) Teams with 15+ hires/year and steady demand High fixed cost; requires onboarding and management time


Fractional Recruiter Hourly or project-based; varies by person Bursty or low-volume hiring Single point of failure; limited tooling and scale


Dover about $4,800 per hire Startups hiring 5-50 roles/year Strongest fit in startup and tech contexts


## When an Agency Recruiter Makes Sense


Agency recruiters work on contingency, so you only pay when a hire is made. They come with a large, active candidate pool already in place and will pre-screen candidates before putting them in front of you.


## The Downsides to Working with an Agency


The[contingency recruiter incentives](https://www.dover.com/blog/30000-intro-dover) create a real structural problem: any candidate in the seat counts as a win, which can push speed over fit. You’ll pay 15 to 25% of starting salary, or nothing if the hire never closes, which is its own problem. Agencies also draw from the pipeline they already have instead of building one scoped to your needs (see[agency vs. recruiter marketplace](https://www.dover.com/blog/startup-agency-recruiting-vs-recruiter-marketplace) ), and they don’t leave behind any hiring infrastructure for your team.[Contingency recruiting fee data](https://www.gofractional.com/blog/contingency-recruiting) shows this 15 to 25% structure has held steady for decades regardless of role complexity or search length.


### Why Dover’s Incentives Are Structured Differently


Dover’s sourcing is scoped to exactly what you need, tuned across 100+ data points and drawing from 300M+ profiles to surface the candidates most likely to be active.


*Learn how*[this founder](https://www.dover.com/case-studies/coverforce) *switched from contingency recruiting to Dover and hired in 3 weeks.*


When sourcing alone falls short, the next step is often bringing in a full-time in-house hire who can own[full-cycle recruiting](https://www.dover.com/blog/full-cycle-recruiting) and drive hiring outcomes end to end.


## When an In-House Recruiter Is Worth the Investment


An in-house recruiter makes sense when you want someone fully embedded in your team and culture, developing hiring best practices from the inside, and building out recruiting infrastructure that stays with the company. It’s also the right call when you want to offload hiring altogether and have a dedicated person driving outcomes, especially if you’re facing a high volume of open roles in the near term.


## The Downsides to Hiring In-House


The downsides are real: you need a steady volume of hiring to keep a full-time recruiter occupied, and finding someone with the right mix of strategic and executional skills is its own challenge. They’ll also need to bring in and set up their own tool stack. And as a[full-time team member](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/human-resources-specialists.htm) , they require onboarding, training, and ongoing professional development, all of which takes time from your plate.


[SHRM’s recruiting benchmarks](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/recruiting-benchmarking) put the average non-executive cost per hire at $5,475, a figure that only makes economic sense when hiring volume is consistent and high.


### How Dover Embeds Without the Full-Time Overhead


Dover’s recruiter works as a true extension of your team. They get to know your culture, calibrate to your hiring bar, and own the process end to end, without the fixed salary, onboarding burden, or management overhead that comes with a full-time hire. Support can scale up or down as your hiring needs shift.


*See how*[this Head of People Ops](https://www.dover.com/case-studies/mozart-data) *pulled in Dover instead of scaling an in-house team.*


When hiring volume is variable or too low to keep a full-time recruiter busy, a fractional arrangement often fits better.


## When a Fractional Recruiter Fits Better


A fractional recruiter is worth considering when hiring volume doesn’t warrant a full-time hire. They often bring specific expertise in your industry niche, and the cost is lower with the option to pause support whenever you need to.


What are the downsides to bringing on a[fractional recruiter](https://www.dover.com/blog/what-is-fractional-recruiter-when-startup-needs-one) ?


The core risk is that a solo fractional recruiter is a single point of failure. If they’re out sick or on vacation, hiring stops with no backup. Their process tends to be more manual and harder to audit, and they’ll need tooling access that may come at an added cost. They also can’t match the capacity or scale of a larger team or service.


### How Dover Removes the Single-Point-of-Failure Risk


Every Dover recruiter is backed by a full support team handling sourcing, scheduling, and same-day phone screens, so a sick day or vacation never stalls your pipeline.


*See how*[this team of 12 hiring managers](https://www.dover.com/case-studies/invoice2go) *relied on Dover to scale from 90 to 130.*


Dover has a track record of success with high-growth companies who have an even higher talent bar.[Founders and execs](https://www.dover.com/founders-and-execs-love-dover) ,[talent leaders](https://www.dover.com/talent-teams-love-dover) , and teams across the startup ecosystem have used Dover to hire. You can[read the case studies](https://www.dover.com/case-studies) to see how.


One factor that often gets overlooked when comparing these models is the underlying tooling infrastructure. Fractional recruiters tend to work best when both the recruiter and the internal hiring team operate from a shared system, one that gives real-time visibility into sourcing activity, candidate flow, and pipeline status. Without that shared layer, coordination happens over email and Slack, sourcing notes live in the recruiter’s own tools, and all of that intelligence disappears when the engagement ends. An ATS that sits underneath the fractional model removes that coordination overhead and means every search builds on what came before it.


## How Dover Fits Into This Decision


The three models above, agency, in-house, and fractional, each carry real structural tradeoffs. Agency recruiters bring speed and an existing candidate pool, but the contingency fee creates an incentive to close quickly instead of closing on the right person. A full-time in-house hire gives you someone fully embedded in your culture, but the loaded annual cost of $85,000 to $170,000 only makes economic sense past roughly 15 hires a year. Fractional support solves the cost problem but introduces its own risk: a single contractor with no backup coverage and a manual process that’s hard to audit.


Dover is built to resolve that bind. The model pairs a free ATS with access to experienced fractional recruiters who work on your roles on a per-hire basis, averaging $4,800 per hire, with no long-term contract required. Each recruiter is backed by a support team that handles sourcing, scheduling, and same-day phone screens, so a sick day or vacation doesn’t stall your pipeline. And because your internal team and the recruiter work from the same shared ATS, there’s no handoff friction or duplicate tooling to manage.


The practical result is a model that behaves like an in-house recruiter, embedded, culture-aware, accountable to your hiring bar, without the fixed cost that makes in-house hiring economically precarious at lower volumes. For startups hiring five to fifty roles a year, that combination is difficult to replicate through any single one of the three traditional models alone.


## FAQs


### Agency recruiter vs Dover: which model actually aligns with a startup’s hiring bar?


Dover’s hourly model removes the placement-fee incentive that pushes contingency recruiters toward speed over fit. You pay for time worked, not the outcome, so there’s no financial pressure to close on a candidate who’s merely available. Agency recruiters draw from an existing pool and move on when a role proves difficult; Dover’s sourcing is scoped to your specific criteria across 100+ data points and continues until you’re satisfied with the results.


### What’s the fastest way to get full-cycle recruiting support without hiring a full-time recruiter?


A fractional model through a service like Dover lets you spin up dedicated recruiter support within days, averaging $4,800 per hire, with no long-term contract required. You get sourcing, screening, scheduling, and closing support without the $85,000 to $170,000 loaded annual cost of an in-house hire, and you can scale hours up or down as hiring needs change.


### How do I know when to hire an in-house recruiter instead of using fractional recruiting support?


SHRM’s recruiting benchmarks put the average non-executive cost per hire at $5,475, a figure that only makes economic sense when hiring volume is consistent and high. The general fit guideline is around 15 to 20 hires per year; below that threshold, a full-time recruiter is likely to sit underutilized, and fractional support tends to be a better match for the actual workload.


### Do fractional recruiters need an ATS to work effectively?


Not strictly, but the absence of a shared ATS creates real coordination overhead. When a fractional recruiter operates in their own tooling and the internal team tracks candidates separately, sourcing notes get duplicated, candidate status lives in multiple places, and all of that pipeline intelligence walks out the door when the engagement ends. A shared ATS, one where the recruiter and the hiring team work from the same pipeline in real time, removes that friction and means each new search starts from an informed baseline instead of zero. Some services, like Dover, pair fractional recruiter access with a free ATS built so both sides work from the same system, which can eliminate the coordination layer entirely.


## Final Thoughts on Choosing the Right Recruiter Model


Recruiter model decisions tend to feel urgent in the moment. A key role is open, the team is stretched, and the cost of waiting is visible. But the model you choose has consequences beyond the immediate hire: it shapes who owns your candidate pipeline, whether sourcing intelligence accumulates or disappears when an engagement ends, and how much fixed cost your runway absorbs between hiring cycles.[Agency, in-house, and fractional recruiting](https://www.dover.com/) each make sense under specific conditions, and those conditions shift as your company grows. The most durable choice is usually the one that matches your actual hiring volume and organizational capacity today, with enough flexibility to change course when those variables shift.
